levels.title: Arrival
story: The supply boat Marigold has put you ashore on Tarrow Skerry, a rock of grass and gannets twelve miles out, to keep its weather station for the winter.
Ines Calder, the keeper you are relieving, went back on the same boat. She left the station in good order and her handover notes on the station's old computer, which is on in front of you.
This computer works by typing. Type ls and press Enter to see what is in this folder.
hints: ls lists what is in the folder you are in. Type ls and press Enter.
There is a file called welcome.txt. cat shows a file: type cat welcome.txt and press Enter.
done: That is the first note read. ls to look, cat to read: most of the work on a computer like this starts with those two.

keeper.welcome.txt:
Welcome to Tarrow Skerry!

Everything you need to know is in the files on this computer.
I have left a note for each thing, a little at a time.
The station's own files are in a folder called station, at the top.

Ines

levels.title: The key board
story: The paint store needs opening: the rust on the instrument enclosure wants touching up before the gales.
There is a board of keys by the door, but the hooks are not labelled. Ines's handover note says where the list is.

goal.text: Which hook does the paint store key hang on? Give the number with answer, as in: answer 3

hints: Read the handover note in this folder first: cat handover.txt
cd moves you into a folder. cd /station goes to the station folder from anywhere; then ls shows what is in it.
From /station, cd stores and then cat keys.txt. Or in one go: cat /station/stores/keys.txt
done: Hook 5. A path like /station/stores/keys.txt names a file from the top of the computer; cd takes you there one folder at a time, and cd .. takes you back up.

Handover, Tarrow Skerry

1. Keys: the board by the door. Which key is which is written in

3. The gannets leave in October and come back in spring.

levels.title: Hidden names
story: The lights went out for a moment last night while the generator changed over, and your torch is nearly flat.
Ines will have kept spare batteries somewhere. She mentioned keeping small notes out of the way.

goal.text: Where are the spare torch batteries? Answer in a few words, as in: answer under the stairs

hints: Read the note in this folder: cat notes.txt
A name that starts with a dot is hidden: ls leaves it out. ls -a shows every name.
There is a file called .batteries. Read it with cat .batteries
done: In the biscuit tin. Names that start with a dot are left out of a plain ls; on real computers that is where settings are kept, out of the way.

story: The mainland calls on the radio: they missed the last reading Ines sent before she left and would like it read out again.

goal.text: What was the wind speed, in knots, at the last reading in the weather log? As in: answer 12

hints: The log is /station/logs/weather.log. head shows the first lines of a file, tail the last.
tail -n 1 shows only the last line: tail -n 1 /station/logs/weather.log
done: 27 knots from the south-west, and the pressure falling: a blow on the way. head and tail are how people look at the start and the end of a log too long to read whole.

levels.title: Foggy days
story: The station keeps a count of days with fog each month. October's was never sent.
Ines wrote one line a day in the October diary. Fog is written in more than one way.

goal.text: How many days in October had fog? As in: answer 4

hints: grep fog finds lines with fog, but not Fog or FOG. grep -i finds all of them.
wc -l counts lines. The | sign sends one command's output into the next: grep -i fog october.txt | wc -l
grep -c does the counting by itself: grep -ic fog october.txt
done: 9 days. The | sign joins small commands into a bigger one: this one found the lines, the next counted them.

levels.title: Tide tables
story: The landing is only safe near high water, and the Marigold is due on the 23rd.
Ines filed the tide tables somewhere in the station folder, which has a great many folders in it. There may be more than one table.

goal.text: What is the time of the first high water on 23 November this year (2026)? As in: answer 10:15

hints: find looks for files by name in a folder and every folder inside it. * stands for anything: find /station -name '*tide*'
Two tables turn up. Only one is for 2026: the path says which.
cat the 2026 one and look along the line for 23 Nov: the first time on it is the answer.
done: 05:02. find saves opening every folder in turn, and the path it gives is often the clue: here, the year.

levels.title: The odd reading
story: The mainland's forecasters have queried one of November's morning barometer readings: they say it cannot be right.
Air pressure at sea level is nearly always between about 950 and 1050 hectopascals. One of the readings is far outside that.

goal.text: On which day of November was the wrong barometer reading written? As in: answer 3

hints: The readings are in /station/instruments/barometer.txt, one a day. Reading thirty numbers by eye is slow.
sort -n puts lines in order by the number at their start; the odd one comes first or last. sort -n barometer.txt | head -n 3
done: The 17th: 101 should have been 1012, a digit left off. Sorting puts what does not belong at one end, where it is easy to see.

levels.title: Who called most
story: The fishing boats that call the station on the radio are given a calendar at Christmas. The one that called most often gets the big one.
Ines wrote the name of every boat that called in November, one name to a line, in the order they called.

goal.text: Which boat called most often in November? As in: answer Fulmar

hints: The names are in /station/logs/calls.txt. uniq -c counts repeated lines, but only lines that are next to each other.
sort first, so that the same names are together: sort calls.txt | uniq -c
Add sort -rn to put the biggest count first: sort calls.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn
done: The Kittiwake, eleven times. sort, then uniq -c, then sort -rn: three small commands that between them count anything listed a line at a time.

levels.title: What needs seeing to
story: Every week the keeper goes round the station with a checklist. Ines did the last round before she left.
Almost everything says ok. Something does not.

goal.text: Which instrument needs seeing to? As in: answer rain gauge

hints: The list is /station/instruments/checks.txt.
grep -v shows the lines that do not hold the text: grep -v ok checks.txt
done: The anemometer, which measures the wind speed: its cups want oil. grep -v hides what is fine and leaves what is not, which is often the quicker way round.

levels.title: Ines's puzzle
story: Sam, the mainland radio operator, has a birthday on Friday. Ines baked a cake before she left and hid it.
She left you a note about where, in a Caesar shift: every letter moved on the same number of places in the alphabet.

goal.text: Where is the cake? Answer in a few words, as in: answer in the boat house

hints: Read cake.txt and clue.txt in this folder.
The clue says the shift is the number of hooks on the key board. wc -l counts the lines in a file: wc -l /station/stores/keys.txt
There are 7 hooks: decode 7 cake.txt
done: Behind the flour in the cold store. A Caesar shift hides a message from a glance but not from anyone who tries all 25 shifts: the Encryption screen under Tools has it, and ciphers that are harder to undo.

levels.title: Handover
story: One last note from Ines, in your home folder.

goal.text: Put Ines's last message together and give it with answer.

hints: Read last.txt in your home folder.
grep -r looks in every file under a folder: grep -r piece /station
Put the pieces in order. Piece 1 says how to undo the rest: echo XLI WXEXMSR MW CSYVW | decode 4
done: THE STATION IS YOURS. You have found your way round a whole computer by typing: folders, paths, reading, searching, counting, sorting and pipes. Real terminals work the same way.
Every level can be played again from the list under the terminal.
